title: Jensen Huang’s Vision for Europe Runs on Plug-In Data Centers
content:
Jensen Huang outlined his vision of Europe’s future at Nvidia’s global conference in Berlin on Wednesday. It consists of robotics, AI agents, and modular data centers, with Nvidia unsurprisingly powering it all.
“To be part of this AI economy, you don’t want to just be consuming the AI. You want to be producing the AI,” he told the 4,000-strong crowd at Nvidia’s GTC. “We can do all of that here in Europe.”
The last GTC, held in San Jose, California, in March, was all about AI inference and more efficient compute. Seven months later, the focus has switched to power, agents, and physical AI. There were even some cute little Microduck robots—made by recent Nvidia acquisition Hugging Face—doing Huang’s bidding at the end of his 90-minute pitch.
Huang’s first big announcement was a modular “AI factory” called the DSX Pod. It is a “plug-and-play” option for building AI data centers, with everything arriving already assembled in a large metal container and packed with Nvidia’s latest Vera Rubin compute racks. It can be brought online in 14 days, instead of taking months or years to construct. That may come in especially handy in Europe, where infrastructure projects are notoriously slow. Huang said the DSX Pod would also slash the amount of time compute sits idle in a data center as it will come online quicker. “This is a complete transformation,” he said.
The speech, delivered at Berlin’s Tempodrom, a venue inspired by a circus tent with the lighting of a gamer’s den, veered between selling laptops and sweeping predictions, with Nvidia presented as the fundamental technology provider to every industry. At one point, two Greenpeace protesters stood up and unfurled a banner reading “Clean up your dirty business.” Huang told his security team to “Go easy” as they were marched out.
Humanoid robotics will be the “next great industry,” Huang said, arguing that Europe was well-placed to lead on it due to its manufacturing heritage. But physical AI goes way beyond robotics, Huang pointed out, explaining that even telecom operators are adding Nvidia GPUs to their cell towers. He also announced partnerships with European carmakers VW and Mercedes on AVs.
Nvidia is making a similar move in humanoid robotics, with Huang announcing the launch of a full-stack robotics platform to standardize configuration. It also plans to release a preconfigured reference robot, Agile One, available in the first quarter of next year, to help developers start building physical AI systems. “This is your great opportunity,” he said.
On model usage, Huang predicted: “Every company in the future will use both closed models as well as open models that you customize.” He showcased Nvidia’s own open-source models as hitting frontier performance once customized on an organization’s proprietary data.
He also predicted that agents would mean there will be more users of software tools than ever before, and said agents’ reasoning, iteration, and tool use are pushing token consumption and demand for computing—and Nvidia GPUs—higher.
In case the 90-minute speech was too technical, it ended with an AI-generated Eurovision song summing up what Huang had just announced. The speech was easier to follow, to be fair.

report.summary: At GTC Berlin, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang pitched modular plug-in AI data centers, robotics, and agents as the foundation for Europe’s AI economy.
report.background: Nvidia’s Berlin GTC comes as Europe tries to close its AI infrastructure gap and assert “sovereign AI” ambitions. European data-center projects often face slow permitting, grid constraints, and lengthy construction, while the US and China scale compute faster. Nvidia is also widening its story beyond chips: at its March GTC it emphasized inference efficiency, but in Berlin it shifted toward power, AI agents, and physical AI. Europe’s manufacturing and automotive strengths make robotics and industrial AI attractive. By offering plug-and-play AI factories and robotics platforms, Nvidia aims to embed its full stack—GPUs, software, models, and reference designs—across European industries before rivals or local chipmakers gain ground.
key_points: The DSX Pod is a containerized “AI factory” packed with Nvidia’s Vera Rubin compute racks. Nvidia says it can come online in 14 days rather than months or years, addressing Europe’s notoriously slow infrastructure buildout and reducing idle compute time. It is plug-and-play, but also tightly tied to Nvidia’s hardware and software stack.

Huang called humanoid robotics the “next great industry” and argued Europe can lead because of its manufacturing heritage. Nvidia announced a full-stack robotics platform to standardize configuration and a preconfigured reference robot, Agile One, due in Q1. It also highlighted telecom operators adding GPUs to cell towers and AV partnerships with VW and Mercedes.

On models, Huang predicted every company will use both closed models and open models customized on proprietary data. He showcased Nvidia’s open-source models reaching frontier performance after customization. He also argued agents’ reasoning, iteration, and tool use will increase token consumption and demand for Nvidia GPUs.

Huang urged Europe to produce AI rather than merely consume it, positioning Nvidia as the foundational technology provider across data centers, robotics, automotive, and telecom. The message aligns with Europe’s sovereign-AI push, but it also risks deepening dependence on one US chip and software supplier.

The event’s focus on power was underscored by Greenpeace protesters unfurling a “Clean up your dirty business” banner. Faster modular data centers may ease deployment bottlenecks, but they do not resolve concerns about energy demand, grid pressure, and the climate footprint of AI infrastructure.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Nvidia’s DSX Pod could accelerate data-center buildouts and normalize containerized AI factories, strengthening Nvidia’s full-stack advantage while pressuring cloud and infrastructure rivals. For developers, Agile One, robotics platforms, and customized open models lower the barrier to physical-AI and agent experimentation, but they also raise lock-in concerns around Nvidia’s ecosystem. For regular users, the vision implies more capable agents, robots, and AI services arriving faster in Europe—alongside higher energy demand and continued scrutiny of AI’s environmental cost. Europe’s ability to convert manufacturing strength into physical-AI leadership will depend on power, skills, and whether local alternatives can compete.
report.tools: Follow Nvidia’s DSX Pod, Vera Rubin, Agile One, and Isaac robotics stack. For open-source experimentation, look at ROS 2, NVIDIA Isaac ROS, Hugging Face LeRobot, and inference servers such as vLLM or TensorRT-LLM; they let developers prototype physical-AI and agent workloads without waiting for proprietary hardware.
